quote: Die Entfernung in meinem Sinne ist war- scheinlich genau das elliptische Integral 3ter Gattung.
english: The distance in my sense is probably exactly the elliptic integral of the third kind.
topic: The page bounds the genus of algebraic relations between transcendental entire functions, sketches elliptic functions as non-Euclidean geometry on a genus-1 ring with distance as the elliptic integral of the third kind, and asks whether 11 consecutive ones occur in the decimal expansion of pi.

triage.modern_statement: This is not a well-posed research question. My best reading: Hilbert wanted to treat elliptic functions as a kind of non-Euclidean geometry on a genus-1 surface (a torus, his 'ring'). He guessed that the right distance between two points there is given by the normalized elliptic integral of the third kind, the elliptic case of the abelian integral with logarithmic poles. His own 'distance in my sense' is presumably the Hilbert projective metric, where distance is the logarithm of a cross-ratio. If so, the guess amounts to this: on a curve of genus 1, the integral of the third kind plays the role of 'log of a cross-ratio'. The page does not define the metric, the axioms or the extremal property he had in mind, so no precise theorem or conjecture can be pulled out of it.
triage.answered_by: No one, as a specific problem. I found no source that discusses or settles this note. The analogy behind it is standard classical theory: the abelian integral of the third kind on a Riemann surface can be written as a generalized cross-ratio using the Schottky–Klein prime form, and it is the log-derivative of the prime form. These are classical results (Klein, Schottky) and do not answer Hilbert's metric question.

evidence.claim: Hilbert's metric (the Hilbert projective metric) defines the distance between two points as the logarithm of a cross-ratio of four points. This is probably what 'distance in my sense' refers to.

On a general Riemann surface, the third-kind differential ω_{a-b} can be written as a kind of cross-ratio, allowing multivaluedness, using the Schottky–Klein prime form E(z,ζ). It can also be recovered as a logarithmic derivative of the prime form. This is the cross-ratio analogy Hilbert seems to have had in mind.

Hilbert used 'non-Euclidean' in a very broad sense, for many geometries that keep some of the Euclidean axioms. Distance as a logarithm of a cross-ratio is central to the setting of his fourth problem.

triage.why: The note is a one-line heuristic guess. 'Distance in my sense' and the intended geometry on the genus-1 ring are not defined on the page, so I could not reconstruct a precise statement to call solved or open. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. I found no literature that addresses this note. The cross-ratio and prime-form link above shows the idea makes sense structurally, but that is my own connection and no source ties it to Hilbert's remark. Hilbert-type metrics, and generalized cross-ratios and prime forms on Riemann surfaces, are both still studied today, but I found nothing aimed at this particular question.
